passage: In a small flat in Valencia, Pablo pushes a toy car along the floor and under the sofa. Noa, one, follows it with her eyes, head turning. When it vanishes, she doesn't stare at the spot where it went in. She crawls straight to the other end of the sofa and waits, eyes on the gap. The car rolls out; she squeals and grabs it. Pablo tries again, faster. This time her eyes are already on the far side.

qa.q: Where did Noa wait for the car?
qa.a: At the other end of the sofa, watching the gap.

qa.q: What does Noa crawling to the far end suggest she expected?
qa.a: She expected the car to come out on the other side, and her squeal when it did shows she was excited and delighted to be right.

qa.q: How could Pablo make this game a little harder for Noa?
qa.a: He could use a longer tunnel or change the speed, and see whether she still waits at the right end.

qa.q: What is it like for Pablo to watch Noa's eyes move ahead of the car?
qa.a: He probably feels delighted to see her start predicting where things go. 😊

grounding: Shows a toddler following a moving toy with her eyes and predicting where it will come out.

passage: I'm Sharmila, and I was on the terrace with my baby sister Sonali when the kites were up. She kept her eyes on a green kite as it dipped and rose. When it swooped behind the water tank, she turned her head and stared at the other side of the tank, mouth open, before it came back into view. Then she bounced and pointed. I can't know what she was thinking, but it looked like she knew where it would pop out.

qa.q: Where did the green kite go out of view?
qa.a: Behind the water tank.

qa.q: What does Sonali's bouncing and pointing suggest she felt?
qa.a: She seemed excited, maybe pleased that the kite came back where she was looking.

qa.q: How could Sharmila play with Sonali using this skill?
qa.a: She could roll a ball behind a box and let Sonali watch for where it comes out.

qa.q: How might their parents react if Sharmila told them about the kite?
qa.a: They would likely be pleased to hear Sonali is following moving things and guessing where they will show up.

grounding: Shows a sibling noticing a toddler track a kite and look ahead to where it reappears.

passage: Sunday: from their window, Farhan, fourteen months, hears the train and looks around, but the carriages have passed by the time he finds them. Vinita, his mother, points. Wednesday: he catches the engine and follows it until it disappears behind the water tower, then looks at her. The next Monday, when it slides behind the tower, his eyes jump to the other side and wait. The engine appears. He squeals and slaps the windowsill.

qa.q: What does the train disappear behind?
qa.a: The water tower.

qa.q: What might Farhan have been expecting when his eyes jumped to the other side?
qa.a: He seemed eager and excited, expecting the engine to come out there, and he squealed with delight when it did.

qa.q: How did Vinita help early on, and why did it work?
qa.a: By pointing to the train, she showed him where to look, so he could start following it himself.

qa.q: What would change if Vinita never stood with him at the window?
qa.a: Farhan would have fewer daily chances to practise following the train, and she would miss seeing his progress.

grounding: Shows a toddler's eye tracking improving over days until he anticipates where the train will reappear.

passage: In the Mumbai flat, Maria, ten months, lay on the mat while her uncle Imran rolled a red ball slowly across the floor. Her eyes followed it all the way to the sofa. When it rolled underneath, she stared at the other side, waiting. The ball came out. She kicked her legs and squealed. Imran rolled it again. This time Maria looked at the other side before it even disappeared.

qa.q: What colour was the ball Imran rolled?
qa.a: The ball was red.

qa.q: What does Maria kicking and squealing suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she was excited and happy when the ball came out where she expected.

qa.q: How can Imran keep building Maria's tracking skills?
qa.a: He can keep rolling toys slowly behind objects so she can practise predicting where they'll come out.

qa.q: How might Imran feel watching Maria look ahead the second time?
qa.a: He might feel delighted and amazed that she had already learned where the ball would reappear.

grounding: Shows a baby following a moving ball with her eyes and anticipating where it will reappear.

passage:
"Arnab, watch the train!"
Manjula, Arnab's mother, pushes the toy train through a cardboard tunnel.
Arnab, eleven months, stares at the tunnel entrance.
"Where did it go?"
His eyes slide to the other end.
"Choo-choo!" The train pops out.
Arnab squeals and bangs the floor.
"Again?"
This time Arnab looks at the far end before the train even goes in.
"You knew!" Manjula laughs.

qa.q: What did Manjula push through the tunnel?
qa.a: She pushed a toy train through a cardboard tunnel.

qa.q: What does Arnab looking at the far end before the train goes in suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he expected it to come out there, and was excited to see it.

qa.q: How can Manjula keep supporting Arnab's tracking?
qa.a: She could vary the speed and path of the train so he keeps practising following and predicting.

qa.q: How does Manjula feel when Arnab looks ahead?
qa.a: She's delighted and laughs, seeing that he has learned where the train will appear.

grounding: Shows a baby tracking a moving train and anticipating where it will reappear.

passage:
Note from Tejas, playgroup leader, Friday
We rolled a ball through the cardboard tunnel today. Pradeep (15 months) watched it go in, then turned his head to the far end before it came out, and squealed when it did. On the third roll I paused it inside; he stared at the exit, then crawled over to peek in. With the toy train he followed it round the whole track with his eyes. Next week: two tunnels.

qa.q: What did they roll through the cardboard tunnel?
qa.a: A ball.

qa.q: What does Pradeep's squeal when the ball came out suggest?
qa.a: He was delighted that it showed up where he expected, as if his guess had come true.

qa.q: Why might two tunnels be a good next step for Pradeep?
qa.a: It gives him a slightly harder guess about where the ball will appear, stretching his tracking without making it frustrating.

qa.q: What would change if Tejas never paused the ball inside?
qa.a: Tejas wouldn't have seen that Pradeep goes looking for it, which shows he knows it is still there.

grounding: Shows a toddler following a moving ball and train with his eyes and looking ahead to where the ball will come out.

passage: Every evening the goods train passed behind the sugarcane fields of their village, and Rekha carried her daughter Ankita to the edge of the yard to watch. At first Ankita only stared at the engine. Now, at twenty months, she follows it with her eyes until it slips behind the water tank, then swings her head to the other side of the tank and waits, pointing. When the engine appears again, she bounces in Rekha's arms and shouts, "Aa-gaya!"

qa.q: What does the train slip behind?
qa.a: The water tank.

qa.q: What does Ankita's pointing at the other side of the tank suggest?
qa.a: She expects the train to come out there and feels eager as she waits for it.

qa.q: How could Rekha play with this skill at home?
qa.a: Roll a ball behind a box and let Ankita guess where it will come out.

qa.q: What is it like for Rekha to share this evening routine?
qa.a: It is likely a warm, happy moment, since she gets to see Ankita's new understanding up close.

grounding: Shows a toddler tracking a train with her eyes and looking ahead to where it will reappear.

passage: Snow had fallen overnight in Hamburg, and Esther pulled her grandson Felix, two, along the path on a small sled. A red bus crossed the end of the street and disappeared behind the bakery. Felix twisted round, eyes fixed on the far corner of the bakery, and held his breath. When the bus rolled out again he shouted "Bus!" and kicked his boots against the sled. Esther stopped so he could watch the next one.

qa.q: What did the red bus disappear behind?
qa.a: The bakery.

qa.q: Why did Felix hold his breath looking at the far corner?
qa.a: He expected the bus to reappear there and felt excited, waiting for it.

qa.q: How did Esther support Felix's interest, and what else could she try?
qa.a: She stopped so he could watch; she could also ask "Where will it come out?" to invite his guesses.

qa.q: How might Esther feel on this snowy walk?
qa.a: Probably amused and pleased to see him so absorbed, even if the walk takes longer.

grounding: Shows a toddler watching a bus vanish and looking ahead to where it will reappear on a winter walk.

passage: I'm Ishita, Zainab's neighbour. On Uttarayan everyone flies kites in our Ahmedabad pol. Zainab is one and a half. Her Abbu held her while a red kite dipped behind the water tank. She stared at the tank, not at the sky, waiting. When the kite popped out the other side, she squealed and pointed. It went behind the tank three times. Every time, she was already looking at the right side before it came out.

qa.q: What colour was the kite?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: What did Zainab's squeal suggest when the kite reappeared?
qa.a: Zainab felt delighted and excited that the kite came back where she expected.

qa.q: How could Zainab's family play with this new skill?
qa.a: They could play simple hide-and-reappear games, like rolling a ball behind a cushion, and cheer when she looks to the right place.

qa.q: How does Ishita see Zainab's watching?
qa.a: Ishita is impressed and amused, noticing that Zainab looks to the right side before the kite appears.

grounding: On the kite festival, a neighbour sees a toddler track a kite and anticipate where it will reappear.

passage:
First rainy Sunday. Hemant, Ojas's Dadu, set up a toy train on the floor with a cardboard tunnel. Ojas, fourteen months, watched the engine go in and stared at the spot where it vanished.
Next Sunday, still raining. When the engine went in, Ojas's eyes slid ahead to the far end. He crawled there and waited.
The third Sunday. Ojas pointed at the far end before the train even entered, and laughed when it came out right under his finger.

qa.q: What was the tunnel made of?
qa.a: Cardboard.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel when the train came out under his finger?
qa.a: Ojas felt delighted and excited, laughing because he had guessed right.

qa.q: How did Dadu's simple game support Ojas's development?
qa.a: Repeating the same train and tunnel each week let Ojas practise following it and predicting where it would come out.

qa.q: How might Hemant feel watching Ojas point before the train entered?
qa.a: Hemant would likely feel proud and pleased, seeing his grandson learn to anticipate.

grounding: Over three rainy Sundays, a toddler learns to anticipate where his grandfather's toy train will emerge.

passage: At the Christmas fair on Park Street, Kalyani bought a bubble wand, and Harsha, sixteen months, sat in his pram under the strings of lights. She blew a big bubble. His eyes followed it up, past the lamp post. When it drifted behind a balloon seller, he leaned sideways, looked to the other side, and caught it again as it came out. Pop. He gasped and slapped the pram. "Ba!" He wanted another.

qa.q: What did Kalyani buy at the fair?
qa.a: A bubble wand.

qa.q: What did Harsha's gasp and slap of the pram show?
qa.a: Harsha felt surprised and delighted when the bubble popped, and eager for another.

qa.q: How could Kalyani keep playing with Harsha's tracking?
qa.a: Blow bubbles slowly in different directions and let him follow and find them, naming them as they go.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel watching him lean to find the bubble?
qa.a: Kalyani would probably feel amused and proud of his sharp eyes.

grounding: At a Christmas fair in Kolkata, a toddler follows a bubble with his eyes and finds it again after it disappears.

passage:
"Mehak, watch him," Siddharth said. It was Holi afternoon, and a small ball of dried gulal was rolling across the courtyard.

Their son Ishir followed it with his eyes.

"It went behind the tulsi pot," Mehak said.

Ishir didn't look where it vanished. He looked at the other side of the pot.

"He's waiting for it to come out!"

The ball rolled out. Ishir squealed and crawled after it.

qa.q: Where did the ball go?
qa.a: It went behind the tulsi pot.

qa.q: How did Ishir feel when the ball rolled out?
qa.a: Ishir was delighted, squealing as he crawled after it.

qa.q: How could Siddharth and Mehak build on this game?
qa.a: Roll balls behind different objects and let Ishir guess where they will come out, cheering when he gets it.

qa.q: What was it like for Mehak to watch Ishir wait at the other side?
qa.a: Mehak was excited and impressed, seeing that he expected the ball to come out.

grounding: On Holi afternoon, a toddler follows a rolling ball with his eyes and anticipates where it will reappear.

passage:
Crèche note, Durga Puja week.

We set up a toy train with a paper tunnel for the Puja display. Jeevan, sixteen months, sat right in front of it.

The first time the train went into the tunnel, he stared at the entrance. By the fourth time, he turned his head to the far end before the train came out, and clapped when it did.

We left the train out for the whole week. — Sarita

qa.q: What did the crèche set up for the Puja display?
qa.a: They set up a toy train with a paper tunnel.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel when the train came out where he expected?
qa.a: Jeevan was happy and excited, clapping when it appeared.

qa.q: How did Sarita support Jeevan's tracking?
qa.a: She left the train and tunnel out all week so he could keep practising.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel noticing the change by the fourth time?
qa.a: Sarita was probably pleased and interested to see his learning grow so quickly.

grounding: A crèche note records a toddler learning to follow a toy train with his eyes and anticipate where it will reappear.

passage:
The mustard fields around the village in Punjab were yellow for Baisakhi. Jyoti sat on the cot outside with Hrithik, who was just over one.

A cat walked along the wall and slipped behind a haystack.

Hrithik watched the hay. Then he turned to the other side of it and waited, mouth open.

The cat came out. Hrithik bounced and pointed, making excited sounds.

Jyoti laughed. "You knew, na?"

qa.q: Where did the cat slip behind?
qa.a: The cat slipped behind a haystack.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel when the cat came out?
qa.a: Hrithik was excited and delighted, bouncing and pointing.

qa.q: How could Jyoti keep encouraging Hrithik's tracking?
qa.a: Point out animals and moving things around the farm and give him time to guess where they will appear.

qa.q: How might Jyoti see Hrithik's waiting?
qa.a: Jyoti is amused and proud, believing he knew where the cat would come out.

grounding: During Baisakhi, a toddler follows a cat with his eyes and anticipates where it will reappear.

qa.a: She pushed a wooden train into the cardboard tunnel.
